profile.name: Jack and Jill
profile.tagline: A competitive partner dance format defined by random pairings and improvisation.
profile.insight: In a Jack and Jill, dancers are paired by chance and must improvise to unknown music, testing their ability to connect with a stranger in real-time.
profile.profile: Created in the 1950s by Jack Carey, the Jack and Jill format challenges dancers to demonstrate social dance skills rather than rehearsed routines. Competitors are randomly matched with partners and must adapt to music selected on the spot. This format emphasizes lead-follow communication, musicality, and the ability to collaborate with a partner under pressure.
profile.profile_long:
The Jack and Jill format emerged in the early 1950s at Hank & Stans in Norwalk, California, conceived by Jack Carey to encourage a wider variety of dancers to enter competitions. Unlike traditional 'showcase' competitions that rely on fixed, pre-arranged choreography, the Jack and Jill format is designed specifically to test the core social dance skills of improvisation, musicality, and partner connection. Participants enter the competition as individuals, and partners are assigned randomly, forcing dancers to adapt to the specific characteristics of a partner they may have never danced with before.

In the United States, the format is a staple of the West Coast Swing and Lindy Hop communities. Standard rules typically prohibit pre-arranged choreography, costumes, and acrobatic lifts, though these rules may be relaxed at the highest invitational levels. The music is selected at random without prior knowledge by the participants, requiring them to demonstrate 'musicality'—the ability to express the nuances of the song through movement. In preliminary rounds, dancers are often judged individually, while in the finals, the focus shifts to the couple's ability to function as a cohesive unit.

Technical evaluation often follows the 'TTT' principle: timing, ensuring steps are in rhythm; technique, focusing on the quality of lead and follow; and team-work, the ability of the pair to communicate and enjoy the dance. Variations of the format exist to accommodate different gender dynamics, such as Jill'n'Jack, Jill'n'Jill, Jack'n'Jack, and the gender-neutral 'Pat and Chris' format. While the competition can be intense, the atmosphere is generally intended to be social and lighthearted, with the random nature of the pairings often compared to the unpredictability of sports.

sections.origins_and_history: The format was created by Jack Carey in the early 1950s at Hank & Stans in Norwalk, California, to encourage more dancers to participate in competitions.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers register individually and are randomly paired with a partner. They dance to music chosen by the DJ at the moment of the performance. In preliminary rounds, dancers are judged individually; in the finals, they are judged as a couple. The format requires constant adaptation to the partner's lead or follow style.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music is selected at random by the DJ. The style depends on the specific dance community hosting the event, such as West Coast Swing, Lindy Hop, Brazilian Zouk, or Salsa.
sections.costume_and_setting: Costumes are generally not allowed in standard competitions. Dancers typically wear numbered bibs to help judges identify them. Elegant attire is encouraged, while unsuitable footwear or casual clothing like jeans are often discouraged.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The format is used in dance conventions and competitions to test social dance skills. It is intended to be a fun, social experience rather than a rigid performance.
sections.regional_variants: Variations include Jill'n'Jack, Jill'n'Jill, Jack'n'Jack, and Pat'n'Chris. Competition formats include 'All Skate', 'Jam', and 'Spotlight'.

teaching.formation: Couples are randomly matched and dance in a social dance setting or on a competition floor.

music_profile.sound_description: Music is selected at random by the DJ; dancers must adapt to whatever genre or tempo is played.

movement_profile.formation_and_space: Couples are randomly paired and move within the competition floor space.
movement_profile.partnering: Requires high-level lead and follow skills to coordinate with a randomly assigned partner.
movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Acrobatic elements such as lifts are generally not allowed unless deemed safe by judges.
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Pre-arranged choreography, costumes, and unauthorized acrobatic lifts.

claims.text: The TTT rule is one of the most common, focusing on timing, technique, and team-work.
claims.quote: Une des règles les plus courantes est celle du TTT : timing : les pas sont en rythme (en général, faire un contretemps est fatal) ; technique : qualité du guidage et propreté de la danse ; team-work : capacité des danseurs à se comprendre et à s'amuser.
